title: BookingService core modules
idea: The core modules are `BookingService` and the repositories it calls: the service enforces each booking rule in a fixed order, and storage stays behind interfaces.

analogy.text: A hotel front desk checks your dates make sense, confirms the room exists, reads that room's page in the ledger, and only then writes your name.
analogy.breaks: A clerk can bend a rule; the service never does.

points: Build bottom-up: entities, then repositories, then the service that orders the rules.
Cheap checks run first: slot shape, then room exists, then the conflict query.
Nothing is saved or numbered until every rule passes; rejections leave no trace.
`synchronized` makes check-then-save atomic in one process; a database needs its own lock.

hero.title: One book call through the rules

steps.caption: `book` is `synchronized`, so this request owns the service until it returns. B1 already holds R1 from 9 to 10.
The slot check costs nothing and needs no storage, so it runs first. 9.5 to 11 is valid.
`findById` confirms R1 exists. An unknown room fails here, before any `Booking` is built.
The service loads R1's bookings and asks the policy. B1 overlaps 9.5 to 10, so the answer is yes.
`RoomTakenException` is thrown. Nothing was saved and the id counter did not move.
The caller gets the code, not a stack trace, and can offer another room or time.
e1 cancels B1. The same request now passes every rule and reaches `save`.
Only now does the id counter move and the booking get saved. B2 returns to the caller.

code.title: Book and cancel
code.caption: The command half of `BookingService`: every rule in order, typed failures, and owner-only cancel.

walk.text: All collaborators arrive through the constructor and are null-checked. The service never creates its own storage.
Slot shape, then room lookup. An unknown room throws `IllegalArgumentException`; a real API maps it to 404.
The candidate is built, then the injected `ConflictPolicy` judges it against this room's bookings only.
The counter moves and save runs last, so a rejected request leaves the counter and repository untouched.
`cancel` loads the booking and compares owners before removing. Ownership is a rule, not a UI check.
The in-memory repository uses a `TreeMap`, so `forRoom` returns bookings in a stable order.
The run shows a clash, a bad slot, a stranger's cancel, then the freed slot rebooked.

code.title: Search, with checks
code.caption: The query half, `searchFree`, tested at its edges with a hand-written check runner.

walk.text: A capacity below one is a caller bug, so it fails fast with a clear message.
A probe booking reuses the same `ConflictPolicy` as `book`. Search and book can never disagree.
Capacity is a minimum. The cheaper capacity test runs before the repository query.
`RoomRepository` is trimmed to one method here, so a lambda serves as the fake.
Each check targets an edge: minimum capacity, overlap, a touching slot, and an empty result.

pitfalls: Saving before the conflict check, then deleting on clash, leaves a window where two bookings exist.
Incrementing the id counter before validation creates gaps that look like lost bookings in audits.
Writing a second overlap rule inside search makes search show rooms that book then rejects.

quiz.q: In BookingModule, what does line 18 print?
options: NOT_OWNER: e2 does not own B1
quiz.why: `cancel` finds B1, sees its `employeeId` is e1, and throws `NotOwnerException`. `attempt` prints its code and message.

takeaway: Order the rules cheapest first, and save only after every rule passes.

starters: Is synchronized on the whole service too coarse for many rooms?
How would book stay correct with two app servers and one database?
Why does searchFree reuse ConflictPolicy instead of its own loop?
